Return only the most likely original continuation, without repeating the supplied text, adding headings, quoting the prompt, or explaining your approach. This is a text-continuation task. Generate at least 1496 characters of continuation text after repeated whitespace is collapsed. Aim for about 2095 characters (approximately 264 whitespace-separated words). This is a minimum-length request, not a maximum. If the next sentence or paragraph ends before the minimum is reached, continue the case narrative. Do not pad, repeat, add a preface, or discuss the requested length.

A 58-year-old female office worker was admitted to the Department of Neurology at the First People’s Hospital of Yunnan Province on June 12, 2026, with a six-month history of nocturnal behavioral abnormalities. The episodes, attributed to chronic work-related stress, occurred repeatedly between 4:00 AM and 6:00 AM and were characterized by behaviors such as folding blankets, standing and walking, wiping tables, shouting, repeatedly touching her head, and thrashing in bed. These episodes were accompanied by urinary incontinence. Family members’ attempts to arouse her during the episodes were ineffective, and she frequently fell out of bed. The patient experienced no choking or awakening during the episodes and had complete amnesia for the events upon waking. She had significant snoring with a loud volume, and family members reported observed apnea episodes. She typically woke spontaneously around 7:00–8:00 AM and felt normal afterward. Since symptom onset, she reported decreased energy and concentration, with a weight loss of approximately 5 kg over the preceding six months. The patient had a 10-year history of hypertension, managed with regular oral irbesartan. She had been diagnosed with moderate obstructive sleep apnea syndrome one month prior but had not received specific treatment. Family members reported multiple episodes of nocturnal hypoglycemia, with documented blood glucose levels around 2.0 mmol/L. She denied any history of diabetes mellitus, prior surgeries, trauma,

message.content:
or head trauma, and no history of psychiatric illness or substance use. Her family history was unremarkable for neurological or endocrine disorders. On physical examination, her blood pressure was 138/86 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, and body mass index was 24.3 kg/m². Neurological examination revealed no focal deficits; higher cortical functions, including language, memory, and orientation, were intact. Cranial nerve examination was normal, and motor and sensory examinations showed no abnormalities. Deep tendon reflexes were symmetric, and plantar responses were flexor bilaterally.

Polysomnography performed during the admission revealed moderate obstructive sleep apnea with an apnea-hypopnea index of 24 events per hour, with significant desaturations. Notably, continuous monitoring captured episodes of complex motor activity during non-REM sleep stages, accompanied by marked bradycardia and a drop in blood pressure. Simultaneous continuous glucose monitoring documented recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia, with nadir values of 1.8 mmol/L temporally correlated with the behavioral episodes.

Laboratory investigations revealed fasting blood glucose of 2.1 mmol/L, with elevated fasting insulin at 42.3 μIU/mL (reference range 2.6–24.9) and a C-peptide level of 4.8 ng/mL (reference range 1.1–4.4). The proinsulin level was markedly elevated at 186 pmol/L (reference range 5–76). A 72-hour fasting test was performed, during which the patient developed symptomatic hypoglycemia at 36 hours with a blood glucose of 1.9 mmol/L, concurrent insulin of 58.1 μIU/mL, and C-peptide of 5.2 ng/mL. The sulfonylurea screen was negative.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography identified a 2.3 cm hypervascular mass in the body of the pancreas. Endoscopic ultrasound confirmed a well-circumscribed lesion with no evidence of local invasion or lymphadenopathy.

The patient was diagnosed with an insulinoma. She underwent a distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy. Postoperative blood glucose levels normalized within 24 hours, and the nocturnal behavioral episodes ceased entirely. At a six-month follow-up, the patient reported no recurrence of nocturnal episodes, stable weight, and improved daytime energy. The final pathology confirmed a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, grade 1, with negative margins.
